Juvenile specimens of Odontocymbiola magellanica emerge from their egg capsules with a shell measuring just 0.69 centimeters [Lb = 0.69 centimeters] at the aperture, a size that reflects the limited nutritional provision of the encapsulated yolk reserves that sustain the earliest post-hatching period. This initial shell dimension, derived from comparative allometry with the related volutid Adelomelon beckii, positions the neonates among the smaller-bodied recruits within the Volutidae family, a pattern consistent with the relatively low fecundity and high maternal investment characteristic of this lineage. Upon hatching, these individuals commence a benthic existence, immediately beginning to forage on small invertebrate prey in the soft sediment habitats characteristic of the southern Patagonian shelf. Field surveys indicate that the period following emergence is critical, as juveniles face high mortality from crustacean predators before they attain a size refuge. The relatively modest birth length nevertheless confers the advantage of reduced metabolic demand during the early, vulnerable stages of independent life. Recruitment success in this species appears tightly linked to the availability of polychaete worms and small bivalves, which constitute the primary diet of the youngest volutes. Observations from laboratory rearing studies further indicate that growth during the first few months is slow, with individuals adding only about 0.5 to 1.0 millimeters of shell length per month under optimal food conditions, a rate that underscores the conservative growth strategy of this cold-water gastropod.

As individuals grow, they progress through a prolonged sub-adult phase characterized by steady shell accretion and gradual thickening of the columella. Sexual maturation in females is attained at a shell length of approximately 10.3 centimeters [Lp = approximately 10.3 centimeters], a developmental milestone that marks the onset of gametogenesis and the capacity for reproductive investment. This size at puberty, recorded from dissected wild specimens collected during the austral summer, aligns well with the pattern observed in other large-bodied neogastropods where a substantial somatic foundation must be established before reproductive allocation becomes feasible. The transition to reproductive maturity involves not only gonadal development but also a notable shift in resource allocation, as feeding rates increase to support the simultaneous demands of continued growth and egg production. Histological examinations of ovarian tissue from females at this shell length reveal active oogenesis, confirming that the 10.3 centimeter [Lp = 10.3 centimeter] benchmark represents a genuine physiological threshold rather than a simple morphological correlate. Males in this species reach sexual maturity at a slightly smaller size, though the difference is minor relative to the overall growth trajectory.

Adult Odontocymbiola magellanica eventually achieve a maximum shell length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters], a dimension that places this species among the larger volutids inhabiting the temperate waters of the southwestern Atlantic. Corresponding to this ultimate shell size, the maximum wet body mass attained by fully grown individuals is 410 grams [Wwi = 410 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions applied to specimens collected during trawl surveys. The relationship between shell length and tissue mass in this species follows a typical positive allometric pattern, meaning that larger individuals carry disproportionately greater soft-tissue mass relative to shell weight. This allometry has implications for reproductive output, since fecundity is often limited by the available coelomic space for egg production in gastropods. At their terminal size (20 cm) [Li = 20 cm], adults exhibit a robust, heavy shell with a thickened outer lip, characteristic of a long-lived iteroparous predator. The energetic investment required to reach this final dimension is substantial, encompassing multiple years of continuous feeding on a diet dominated by other molluscs and echinoderms.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan for Odontocymbiola magellanica extends to 20 years [am = 20 years], a longevity that reflects the characteristically slow life-history pace of large predatory gastropods. This exceptional lifespan (20 years) [am = 20 years] is comparable to that documented for other volutid species in the Magellanic region and is thought to be facilitated by the cold, oxygen-rich waters that reduce metabolic oxidative damage over time at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Mark-recapture studies in the field have corroborated the laboratory estimates, with several tagged individuals being recaptured more than a decade after initial marking. The combination of late sexual maturation, large body size, and extended longevity positions this species firmly within a conservative life-history strategy, where adult survival is prioritized over high annual reproductive output. Senescence in older individuals becomes apparent through reduced feeding activity, thinning of the shell margin, and a decline in gonad mass, typically observed in specimens exceeding 15 years of age.

Under the same thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of Odontocymbiola magellanica involves females producing approximately 2.8 egg capsules per year [Ri = approximately 2.8 egg capsules per year] during the peak spawning period, with individual capsules containing between 5 and 15 fertilized ova. Field observations indicate that spawning activity is concentrated in the late austral spring and early summer, when primary productivity in the water column is at its highest. The high annual encapsulation rate is sustained over a reproductive window lasting several weeks, allowing a single female to deposit hundreds of eggs over the course of a single breeding season. Each egg capsule is a tough, leathery structure affixed to hard substrates such as cobbles or shell debris, providing physical protection to the developing embryos during their prolonged incubation. The cold-water incubation period, lasting approximately 90 days, means that hatching occurs during the warmest part of the summer, maximizing prey availability for the newly emerged juveniles. This reproductive strategy balances high maternal investment per offspring with a moderately paced encapsulation schedule.
